# Editor tour

GodotTrench borrows its habits from TrenchBroom and Hammer, so if you know either, most of this will feel familiar. This page explains how the window is organized and which tool fits which job. The keys are collected in [[shortcuts]].

## The window

Across the top sit the menu bar and the toolbar. The menus group commands by what they act on: **File, Edit, Brush, Mesh, Texture, Terrain, Gameplay, Tools, View, Godot** and **Help**. When you are looking for a command, think about the object first. Under the toolbar, the tool options bar shows the settings of the active tool, or a one line explanation of how to use it.

The middle holds four views, 3D, Top, Front and Side. Drag the point where the dividers cross to resize all four at once. The 2D views show the size of the selection in their corner, which is the quickest way to check that a doorway really is 64 units wide.

Panels dock around the views. By default the Outliner, History and Issues sit on the left, the Inspector, Entities and UV Editor on the right, and Materials and Models along the bottom. Two useful panels are not in the default layout: **Logic** and **Reference**. Open them from *View > Panels*, where *Reset Layout* also puts everything back.

If you cannot find a command, the command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or F1) finds it by name.

## Moving around

In the 3D view, hold the right mouse button to look around and use WASD to move, with Q and E for down and up while you look, and Shift to go three times as fast. The middle button pans, the wheel dollies, and Alt+left drag orbits when nothing is selected. In the 2D views, right or middle drag pans and the wheel zooms towards the cursor.

**F** frames the selection in every view, or the whole map when nothing is selected. For spots you keep coming back to, Ctrl+Shift+1 to 9 stores a camera bookmark and Ctrl+1 to 9 jumps back to it. Bookmarks are saved in the map, so they survive a restart, and undoing does not clear them, they are view state rather than an edit.

F2 cycles the 3D shading between Textured, Flat, Lit Preview and Wireframe. Lit Preview (F3) shows the map's lights, sun shadows, sky and fog, which is a good check before you go to Godot.

## Blocking out with brushes

Brushes are convex solids, and almost everything starts as one. With the **Select** tool (Q), drag on empty space to draw a box, drag a selection to move it, hold Ctrl while dragging to leave a copy behind, and hold Alt in 3D to move vertically. The arrow keys and Page Up and Page Down nudge by one grid step, and `[` and `]` halve and double the grid.

To reshape a selected brush, Shift drag one of its faces in the 3D view to push or pull it, or Ctrl+Shift drag a face outwards to extrude a new brush from it. In the 2D views you resize by dragging the edges of the selection instead.

When a box is not the right shape, **Clip** (C) cuts a brush along a plane: click two or three points, press Tab to choose which side to keep and Enter to cut. That is how slopes, ramps and angled walls are made. **Vertex** (V) moves corners and edges directly, and because the brush is rebuilt as a convex hull afterwards, you can reshape a brush but never dent it. For cylinders, arches, stairs and other shapes that are tedious by hand, use the **Shape Generator** (Ctrl+Shift+B).

CSG combines brushes. **Hollow** (Ctrl+Shift+K) turns a brush into walls. **Subtract** (Ctrl+K) carves the selected brushes out of everything they touch and then deletes them, so the selection acts as a cutter; this is how you punch doorways and windows. **Convex Merge** (Ctrl+M) fuses the selection into one convex brush, and **Intersect** (Ctrl+L) keeps only the overlap.

## Meshes, models and texturing

Brushes are ideal for architecture and poor for anything organic. For that, the **Mesh** tool edits polygon meshes the way Blender does: 1, 2 and 3 switch between vertex, edge and face mode, G, R and S move, rotate and scale, E extrudes, I insets, Ctrl+R adds a loop cut and K is the knife. Select brushes and press Tab (or *Mesh > Edit Mesh*) to convert them and start editing; picking the Mesh tool from the toolbar does not convert anything. Imported models, glTF, OBJ, Blockbench and a few others, appear in the Models panel and are placed by dragging them into a view, or by its **Import…** button when the file is not already under `res://`. Either way you get an editable mesh, not a reference to the file. A prop entity is different, it only stores a `res://` path for Godot to load at runtime, so placing one from outside the project offers to copy the file into `res://models` first.

Texturing happens mostly in the 3D view. Click a thumbnail in Materials to apply it to the selection, or drag it onto a face, holding Shift to cover the whole brush or Alt to drop a decal. The **Texture** tool (Shift+T) is Hammer's face edit mode, in place: drag slides the texture, Ctrl+wheel scales and Alt+wheel rotates. Alt+click is the eyedropper, it picks up a face's material together with its alignment. A plain right click then applies just the material to another face, and Shift+right click applies the material and the alignment, which is how you make a texture run cleanly around a corner.

UV lock (Ctrl+Shift+U) is on by default, so textures stay attached to a brush while you move it. The UV Editor panel handles what the 3D view cannot, for brush faces as well as meshes. The **Paint** tool (P) paints vertex colours onto faces, for dirt, tint and fake lighting.

## Terrain and foliage

*Terrain > Create Terrain...* generates a heightfield from a few parameters, with shapes like hills, mountains, islands and ridges plus erosion, or from a heightmap image. It then switches to **Sculpt** (G) so you can shape it by hand. **Blend** (Shift+G) paints between the terrain's four material layers, and *Auto Paint Layers* does a first pass by slope and height. For a patch of uneven ground inside a brush level, turn a face into a displacement with *Brush > Displacement* and sculpt that instead.

Sculpt, Blend and Paint work on whatever brushes or terrains are selected, or on every editable one when nothing is selected, locked and hidden objects are always left alone either way. Ctrl+wheel resizes the brush for Sculpt, Blend, Paint and Scatter instead of zooming the camera.

**Scatter** (B) paints trees, rocks and grass onto surfaces you choose. Alt+click toggles which surfaces are targets, Shift erases and Ctrl+wheel changes the radius. If your project has no foliage yet, *Terrain > Scatter > Install Nature Models* copies the bundled trees and rocks into `res://godottrench/nature`.

## Gameplay

Point entities come from the Entities panel: drag one into a view, or double click it to place it at the cursor. Brush entities such as doors and triggers are brushes you convert, by selecting them and picking a class from *Create Brush Entity* in the view's right click menu or from *Brush > Brush Entity*. The **Volume** tool (Shift+E) drags out a trigger in one go, and the **Path** tool (Shift+P) clicks down a chain of `path_corner` entities for trains and walking NPCs. The Gameplay menu has ready made setups too: hinged and sliding doors that come with their trigger, lifts, moving platforms, and triggers sized to fit around the selection.

Entities are wired together with outputs, set in the Inspector. For the common case of connecting two entities, select both and use *Gameplay > Logic > Link Two Selected Entities...*. The dialog does not take the entity you clicked first as the source, it takes the one with the lower internal id, so check the direction and press the ⇄ button to swap it if needed. [[io-concepts]] explains what every field means.

To check wiring without starting Godot, open the Logic panel, pick a named entity and one of its outputs, and press **Fire**. It lists every `source.output → target.input` step that would follow, with delays, and marks targets that do not exist in red. Targets that only exist in a running game, such as `!player` or `@enemies`, are shown in blue and not followed further.

The Reference panel shows how to use an entity class from code: GDScript and C# snippets, a class skeleton for writing your own, and the FGD resource. Its **Create in project** button writes the skeleton straight into `res://entities`.

## Keeping a map organized

The Outliner shows the map as a tree of layers, groups and objects. New objects go into the current layer, and clicking a layer makes it current. The eye hides and the lock locks. A layer can also be marked *Omit From Export*, which is handy for reference geometry that should never reach Godot.

Ctrl+G groups the selection. A click selects inside a group and a double click selects the whole group. **Duplicate Linked** (Ctrl+Shift+D) makes a copy that stays in sync with its original, so fixing one window frame fixes all of them. *Edit > Groups > Unlink Groups* breaks the link when one copy needs to differ.

For pieces you reuse across maps, *Edit > Prefabs > Create from Selection...* saves the selection as its own `.gtm` and replaces it with an instance that updates whenever the prefab file changes. Save the map once before you do this, prefab paths are stored relative to it.

## Catching problems early

The Issues panel checks the map as you work: brushes with no volume, faces with no material, outputs aimed at a targetname nothing has, classes with no definition, and a few more. Clicking an issue selects the object and frames it, and most issues have a **Fix** button, with *Fix all* in the header. It only checks that a face has a material name at all, not that the material exists in your Godot project.

The History panel lists every edit. Clicking an older entry undoes back to it, including that entry, and clicking one of the dimmed entries above the marker redoes up to it.

## Saving and recovering

Every save first copies the previous version to `<map>.gtm.bak`, and autosave writes `<map>.gtm.autosave` every three minutes for every tab that has unsaved changes, not only the one you are looking at. The interval is in *File > Preferences*, where 0 turns it off. To recover a saved map, open its autosave file with *File > Open Map* using the "Autosave (recover a map)" filter. An untitled map gets its own autosave file too, and *File > Open Recent* lists those for recovery, which is the only way to find them since they were never saved anywhere you chose.

*File > New Map* (Ctrl+N) and importing a `.map` never throw away unsaved work. If the current map has changes, the new one opens in a tab next to it, and quitting asks about every tab with changes, offering *Save All* or *Discard All* alongside *Cancel*.

Several maps can be open at once as tabs: Ctrl+Shift+N opens a new one, Ctrl+Tab cycles and Ctrl+W closes. The tab bar only appears once two maps are open, and each tab also has its own × to close it. Closing a tab with unsaved changes, by ×, Ctrl+W, the menu or the command palette, asks to save, discard or cancel before it closes.

## Working with Godot and other tools

*Godot > Live Mode* pushes edits into the scene open in the Godot editor before you save, so you can judge lighting and scale in the real renderer while you work. It is off by default. F5 runs the project. [[building-in-godot]] explains the Godot side in detail.

The editor can also run an MCP server, so scripts and AI assistants can build and inspect maps through the same operations you use. Start it with `--mcp` for stdio or `--mcp-http` for a local HTTP server, or turn it on in *File > Preferences*, which also shows the command to register it with Claude Code. The tools are documented in `docs/mcp.md` in the repo.
